objectives: Trace the origins of nutrition science from James Lind's scurvy trial through Lavoisier, Liebig, and Atwater.
Define the kilocalorie and the Atwater factors (4/4/9 kcal per gram for carbohydrate, protein, and fat; 7 for alcohol).
Explain energy balance as the relationship between energy intake and total energy expenditure.

slides.title: From scurvy to calorimetry: the birth of nutrition science
slides.body:
**Nutrition science** is the study of how the nutrients and energy in food sustain life, growth, and health. Although humans have always cared about food, nutrition only became an experimental science in the 18th and 19th centuries through a chain of remarkable investigators.

The first true clinical trial in the history of nutrition was conducted by the Scottish naval surgeon **James Lind** (1716–1794). In **1747**, aboard HMS *Salisbury*, Lind divided twelve scurvy-stricken sailors into six pairs and gave each pair a different supplement — cider, vinegar, seawater, dilute sulfuric acid, a spiced paste, or **two oranges and a lemon**. The pair given **citrus fruit** recovered within days. Lind published his *A Treatise of the Scurvy* in **1753**. Although the active compound (**vitamin C**, ascorbic acid) would not be isolated until **Albert Szent-Györgyi** did so in **1932**, Lind's controlled comparison established the experimental method that defines modern nutrition.

The quantitative foundations were laid by the French chemist **Antoine Lavoisier** (1743–1794), often called the **father of nutrition** and the father of modern chemistry. In the 1780s, working with **Pierre-Simon Laplace**, Lavoisier built an **ice calorimeter** and demonstrated that **respiration is a form of slow combustion** — animals consume oxygen and release carbon dioxide and heat, just as a burning candle does. He measured the heat produced by a guinea pig and showed it matched the heat from burning carbon, proving that the body 'burns' food for energy. Lavoisier was executed during the French Revolution in **1794**, but his insight — that **metabolism is combustion** — anchors the entire field of energy nutrition.

The chemistry of food itself was systematized by the German chemist **Justus von Liebig** (1803–1873) at the University of Giessen. Liebig classified foods into the great chemical categories — **carbohydrates, fats, and proteins** (he popularized the term *protein*, coined by **Gerardus Mulder** in 1838) — and proposed (incorrectly, as it turned out) that protein was the sole fuel of muscular work. Even his errors were productive, because they framed the questions that experimental physiology would spend the next century answering. By the close of the 19th century the stage was set for precise measurement of the energy in food, which is the subject of the next slide.

slides.title: Atwater, the calorie, and the energy in food
slides.body:
The person who turned nutrition into a precise quantitative science was the American chemist **Wilbur Olin Atwater** (1844–1907). After studying in Germany under **Carl von Voit** and **Max Rubner** — pioneers of metabolic measurement — Atwater returned to **Wesleyan University** in Connecticut and, with the physicist **Edward Bennett Rosa**, built the first human **respiration calorimeter** in **1896**. This room-sized chamber sealed a human subject inside while measuring oxygen consumed, carbon dioxide and water exhaled, and heat released. Atwater's experiments confirmed for humans what Lavoisier had shown for animals: the **law of conservation of energy holds for the body** — the energy released by metabolizing food exactly equals the energy that would be released by burning it, once corrections are made for incomplete digestion and excretion.

The unit of food energy is the **kilocalorie** (kcal), also written **Calorie** with a capital C in everyday usage. One kilocalorie is the energy needed to raise the temperature of one kilogram of water by one degree Celsius:

$$1 \text{ kcal} = 1000 \text{ cal} = 4.184 \text{ kJ}$$

From thousands of bomb-calorimeter and digestibility measurements, Atwater derived the **Atwater factors** — the average metabolizable energy yield of each macronutrient:

- **Carbohydrate**: 4 kcal per gram
- **Protein**: 4 kcal per gram
- **Fat**: 9 kcal per gram
- **Alcohol (ethanol)**: 7 kcal per gram

These values appear on every nutrition label in the world and remain the working basis of dietary energy calculation. They are *metabolizable* energy values — lower than the gross heat of combustion, because protein is not fully oxidized (the nitrogen leaves as urea) and because not all of what we eat is absorbed. To estimate the energy content of a food, you multiply the grams of each macronutrient by its factor and sum:

$$E = 4 g_{\text{carb}} + 4 g_{\text{protein}} + 9 g_{\text{fat}} + 7 g_{\text{alcohol}}$$

Atwater's other lasting contribution was nutritional epidemiology: he compiled the first **United States food composition tables** (1896), the ancestor of today's **USDA FoodData Central** database. With these tools, nutritionists could finally answer practical questions: how much energy does this meal contain, and how much does this person need? That second question — energy expenditure — completes the picture of **energy balance**.

slides.title: Vitamins, deficiency diseases, and the principle of energy balance
slides.body:
Atwater's energy science explained *how much* fuel food provides, but it could not explain diseases like scurvy or **beriberi**, which struck people who ate plenty of calories. The missing piece was the discovery of **vitamins** — trace organic compounds essential to life.

The key breakthrough came from the Dutch physician **Christiaan Eijkman** (1858–1930), working in the Dutch East Indies (now Indonesia). In the 1890s he noticed that chickens fed **polished white rice** developed a paralysis resembling the human disease **beriberi**, and that the symptoms vanished when the birds were fed the discarded **rice bran (husk)**. Eijkman had stumbled onto the fact that a substance in the bran — later identified as **thiamine (vitamin B1)** — prevented the disease. For this work he shared the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1929** with **Frederick Gowland Hopkins**, who had independently demonstrated the existence of 'accessory food factors.'

The Polish-born biochemist **Casimir Funk** (1884–1967) gave the new factors their name. In **1912**, believing they were chemical *amines* vital for life, he coined the word **'vitamine'** (vital + amine). The final 'e' was later dropped to **vitamin** when it became clear that not all are amines. That same era saw the American biochemist **Elmer Verner McCollum** (1879–1967) at the University of Wisconsin distinguish, in **1913**, a **fat-soluble factor A** from a **water-soluble factor B** — the first systematic naming scheme for vitamins, which is why we still speak of vitamins A, B, C, and so on.

With macronutrients, energy, and micronutrients all accounted for, modern nutrition rests on a master principle: **energy balance**. The body obeys the first law of thermodynamics. **Energy intake** (the food we eat) is set against **total energy expenditure** (the energy we burn through basal metabolism, the thermic effect of food, and physical activity). The difference is stored or mobilized:

$$\Delta\text{Energy stores} = \text{Energy intake} - \text{Energy expenditure}$$

When intake exceeds expenditure, the surplus is stored, chiefly as **body fat** (each kilogram of adipose tissue holds roughly **7700 kcal**). When expenditure exceeds intake, the body draws on its stores and body mass falls. When the two are equal, weight is stable — a state called **energy equilibrium**. This deceptively simple equation, the direct descendant of Lavoisier's combustion experiments and Atwater's calorimeter, governs everything from athletic performance to the global obesity epidemic, and it is the foundation for every later lesson in this path.

question.question: Why is Antoine Lavoisier often called the 'father of nutrition'?
options: He isolated vitamin C from citrus fruit in 1932 and named it ascorbic acid.
He demonstrated through calorimetry that respiration is a slow form of combustion, showing that the body releases heat by oxidizing food just as a flame oxidizes fuel.
He conducted the first controlled clinical trial by giving scurvy patients oranges and lemons aboard a naval ship.
He coined the word 'vitamine' in 1912 to describe trace factors that prevent deficiency diseases.
question.explanation: Lavoisier (1743–1794), working with Laplace, used an ice calorimeter in the 1780s to show that an animal consumes oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and heat in proportions matching the combustion of carbon. This established that metabolism is essentially controlled combustion — the conceptual basis for measuring food energy. The citrus trial was James Lind (1747); ascorbic acid was isolated by Szent-Györgyi (1932); 'vitamine' was coined by Casimir Funk (1912).

hints: Think about which figure connected breathing and burning.
His tool was a calorimeter, and his big idea was that the body 'burns' food.
slides.workedSolution: Lavoisier's calorimetry experiments proved respiration is combustion: oxygen in, carbon dioxide and heat out, energy conserved. This is why he is credited as the founder of energy nutrition. The other options each describe a real but different scientist — Lind (citrus trial, 1747), Szent-Györgyi (vitamin C, 1932), and Funk ('vitamine', 1912).

question.question: A snack bar contains 30 g of carbohydrate, 10 g of protein, and 12 g of fat. Using the Atwater factors (4, 4, and 9 kcal per gram), how many kilocalories does the bar provide?
question.hint: Energy = 4 × carb grams + 4 × protein grams + 9 × fat grams = 4(30) + 4(10) + 9(12).

question.question: A 355 mL serving of beer contains 13 g of ethanol (alcohol) and 12 g of carbohydrate, with negligible protein and fat. Using the Atwater factor of 7 kcal/g for alcohol and 4 kcal/g for carbohydrate, what is the total energy content in kilocalories?
question.hint: Energy = 7 × alcohol grams + 4 × carb grams = 7(13) + 4(12). Alcohol carries 7 kcal/g — nearly as energy-dense as fat.

question.question: Christiaan Eijkman's experiments with chickens fed polished rice were historically important because they:
options: Proved that protein is the only fuel used by working muscle, confirming Liebig's hypothesis.
Provided early evidence that a specific trace substance in rice bran (later identified as thiamine) prevents beriberi, helping launch the discovery of vitamins.
Established the Atwater factors of 4, 4, and 9 kcal per gram for the three macronutrients.
Showed that the energy released by metabolizing food equals the energy released by burning it.
question.explanation: Eijkman observed that chickens on polished white rice developed a beriberi-like paralysis that was cured by feeding the rice bran. The protective factor was later identified as thiamine (vitamin B1). This work, recognized with the 1929 Nobel Prize (shared with Hopkins), was pivotal in establishing that deficiency diseases are caused by the absence of trace 'accessory food factors' — vitamins. Liebig's protein-fuel idea was wrong; the Atwater factors came from Atwater's calorimetry; and the food-equals-fuel energy equivalence was Lavoisier's and Atwater's work.

hints: The disease in question was beriberi.
The cure was in the part of the rice that polishing removes.
slides.workedSolution: Eijkman's polished-rice experiments linked beriberi to the loss of a substance (thiamine) in rice bran, providing key evidence for the existence of vitamins and earning the 1929 Nobel Prize. This is distinct from the energy work of Lavoisier and Atwater and contradicts Liebig's protein-fuel hypothesis.

question.question: Counseling on energy balance
question.prompt: A 45-year-old office worker tells you he has gained about 0.5 kg per month over the past year despite 'not eating much.' He estimates his daily intake at around 2400 kcal and his total energy expenditure at around 2200 kcal. Using the principle of energy balance and the rule that roughly 7700 kcal are stored per kilogram of body fat, explain to him in plain language why a seemingly small daily surplus produces measurable weight gain over time. Estimate the monthly fat gain his ~200 kcal daily surplus would predict, and discuss why his perception that he is 'not eating much' can still be consistent with positive energy balance.
